clue.text: Enthusiastically welcome every second of farcical object

indicators.note: every second letter of the word farcical is picked, skipping the ones between

parts.note: an object is an aim or goal

explanation.surface: Someone greets a ridiculous thing with every other cheer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'every second of' takes the even letters of 'farcical': A, C, C, L.
explanation.definitionFit: To acclaim is to praise or hail with enthusiasm, a verb in the same form as welcome.

clue.text: Not in favour of current soldier going over the top

indicators.note: in a down entry the soldier's letters sit above the current's letters

parts.note: a soldier ant is a fighting caste ant
I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A soldier goes over the top of the trench, having no stomach for the war.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer, 'going over the top' places ANT above I.
explanation.definitionFit: Being against something is the sense of the preposition, opposed to rather than for.

clue.text: (Grid row 14) one who went over the edge in 16, a captain of discovery

definitions.text: one who went over the edge in 16

explanation.surface: An explorer captain is recalled as someone who fell off a cliff in a comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 16 is COMEDY: Peter Cook was one of the four in the revue Beyond the Fringe, so went 'over the edge' of the fringe; James Cook was the captain who sailed HMS Endeavour and later HMS Discovery.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter Cook starred in Beyond the Fringe, and the naval explorer James Cook commanded ships including Discovery.

clue.text: Male columnists displaying a variety of talents?

indicators.note: a variety is a mixed assortment, so these letters come out jumbled

explanation.surface: Newspaper writers who are men show off an assortment of gifts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variety of' rearranges A plus TALENTS. 'Columnists' looks like journalists but means stone columns carved as men.
explanation.definitionFit: Atlantes are carved figures of men serving as supporting pillars in classical architecture, so male column figures.

clue.text: (Grid row 2) one who went over the edge in 16, in addition having love in heart

definitions.text: one who went over the edge in 16

indicators.note: having means holding something within, so one word takes the other inside it
the zero is placed in the heart, the middle, of the word for in addition

parts.note: more means in addition, as in 'and one more thing'
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A comedian who jumped off the edge also has love at the heart of things.
explanation.walkthrough: Dudley Moore was one of the four Beyond the Fringe stars; 16 is COMEDY.
explanation.definitionFit: Dudley Moore was a member of the Beyond the Fringe revue, the comedy show hinted by the fringe edge.

clue.text: Riot Centre Boy!

parts.note: a hub is the centre of activity
bub is an American address for a boy or young man

explanation.surface: A shout of alarm: a boy in the middle of a riot.
explanation.definitionFit: A hubbub is a noisy uproar or din, close to the sense of a riot as tumult.

clue.text: Cultural agency out of tune with Scots?

indicators.note: the answer is taken out from the middle of the two words joined, their outer letters left behind

explanation.surface: A cultural body is said to be at odds with the music of Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' joins the two words; 'out of' takes the run between the outer letters, leaving T at the front and TS at the back. 'out of tune' wants to be an anagram signal, but no letters need rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization is the UN body for culture and heritage.

clue.text: Doctor obtains old sign of guilt

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: A medic gets hold of an old symptom of a guilty conscience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' is a verb here, rearranging OBTAINS plus OLD.
explanation.definitionFit: A mark of blood left on a garment is classic evidence pointing to guilt in a crime story.

clue.text: However certainly

explanation.surface: Two words of reply, one conceding and one agreeing.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase can mean in any way at all, as in 'however you can', and is also a polite yes.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an emphatic yes, as in 'may I?', and also means in whatever way possible.

clue.text: Divers to do sign need oxygen for so long

indicators.note: divers is the old word for several and sundry, signalling the letters are scattered

parts.note: Leo is a sign of the zodiac
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: Scuba divers on a to-do list need their oxygen supply to last a long time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Divers' is not underwater swimmers but the archaic adjective meaning various, rearranging TO DO into TOOD.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheery British farewell, the same sense as goodbye or see you later.

clue.text: Vegetable — eating much game?

indicators.note: eating means taking something inside, so one word goes into the other

parts.note: a pea is a vegetable
a lot means much

explanation.surface: A vegetable dish eating up a great deal of game meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'game' looks like meat for the table but is the sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Pelota is a Basque ball sport played against a wall, a type of game.

clue.text: Strong liquor served by street bar no end

indicators.note: no end means the final letter is cut off the word for bar

parts.note: an ingot is a bar of metal

explanation.surface: A pub on the street serves strong drink without stopping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bar' looks like a pub but is a metal bar.
explanation.definitionFit: Stingo is an old term for strong ale or beer, so a powerful alcoholic drink.

clue.text: In dialectics animatedly responsible for the demise of cricket?

definitions.text: responsible for the demise of cricket?

indicators.note: doing something animatedly means in a lively, agitated way, stirring the letters up

explanation.surface: A philosophical debate becomes heated enough to kill off a summer sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cricket' looks like the game, but it is the insect, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A pesticide that kills insects, such as a chirping cricket, is described by this adjective.

clue.text: Feeble war baby repeatedly gutted about reversal of plan

parts.note: Nam is short for Vietnam, the war

indicators.note: about means around, so the two copies surround the turned word
repeatedly means the gutted word is used twice over
a gutted word has its insides removed, leaving only the outer letters
reversal means the word for plan is turned back to front

parts.note: a map is a plan

explanation.surface: A weak child born in wartime, the plan having been reversed again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gutted' strips 'baby' to its outer letters, 'repeatedly' doubles them, and 'about' wraps that pair round the turned plan; 'war' is the Vietnam War, not a generic conflict.
explanation.definitionFit: Namby-pamby describes someone weak, sentimental and lacking vigour, matching feeble.

clue.text: 1919 or 1946, say, when a Brit's absorbed a volley of bullets

indicators.note: the Brit has absorbed, i.e. takes in, the jumbled letters

parts.note: pom is Australian slang for a British person

indicators.note: a volley sprays bullets in all directions, so the letters scatter

explanation.surface: A British soldier took a hail of gunfire in a war year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a volley of' rearranges the letters of 'bullets', and the result goes inside the Australian nickname for a Briton.
explanation.definitionFit: Years just after the two world wars ended are examples of the after-war period this Latin term names.

clue.text: Going up to claim pay for unemployed teenager?

indicators.note: to claim means to take hold of, so the climb takes in the payment

parts.note: an ascent is a going up
the dole is British state benefit paid to the unemployed

explanation.surface: An unemployed teenager is going up to sign on for benefits.
explanation.walkthrough: THE DOLE is the British slang for unemployment benefit.
explanation.definitionFit: An adolescent is a young person between childhood and adulthood, the usual sense of teenager.

clue.text: Buffalo Bill lassoes me for amusement

indicators.note: lassoing ropes something in, so one word catches the other inside it

parts.note: Buffalo Bill was the nickname of William Cody, the Wild West showman

explanation.surface: A Wild West showman ropes me in for a bit of fun.
explanation.definitionFit: Comedy is humour or entertainment that causes laughter, a near synonym of amusement.

clue.text: That piece on which control's tight — that's boring!

definitions.text: That piece on which control's tight

explanation.surface: A remark about a dull bit of strict control.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is the metal bar in a horse's mouth used to control it; the second is the drill part that bores holes.
explanation.definitionFit: A bit is the mouthpiece on a bridle for controlling a horse, and also the cutting head of a drill.

clue.text: Workmanlike milkman holds up baker

indicators.note: in a down entry up means the letters are read from bottom to top
the words hold the answer inside them, spanning the join

explanation.surface: A diligent milkman holds up the baker on his round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'baker' looks like a person but is an oven.
explanation.definitionFit: A lime kiln is a furnace that burns limestone to make quicklime, so it bakes material.

clue.text: See 17
The writer's depriving Labour of work burden

parts.note: the writer's means I am, shortened to I'm

indicators.note: depriving something of a word means taking that word away from it

parts.note: in 2011 Labour was the Opposition in the UK Parliament
op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: The author finds that losing Labour's work is a heavy load.
explanation.walkthrough: In 2011 Labour was Britain's main opposition party. 'depriving ... of' removes OP from OPPOSITION.
explanation.definitionFit: An imposition is an unfair demand or load placed on someone, the same as a burden.

clue.text: Take out runner in Chester with permit to enter

indicators.note: to enter means to go inside, so one word goes into the river

parts.note: the River Dee flows through the English city of Chester
to let is to permit

explanation.surface: A runner in Chester is given a pass to compete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'runner' looks like an athlete but a river runs; Chester is a city in north-west England on the Dee.
explanation.definitionFit: To delete is to remove or strike out text, a synonym of take out.

clue.text: Resident cloth rep hit edge of kerb before stop sign

indicators.note: before means the kerb letter comes ahead of the stop
hit means damaged and so knocked out of shape
the edge here is the final letter of the word kerb

parts.note: to end is to stop
Aries is a sign of the zodiac

explanation.surface: A sales rep crashes his car into a kerb just before a stop sign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hit' rearranges REP into PRE. 'cloth' is the clergy.
explanation.definitionFit: Prebendaries are canons holding a stipend from a cathedral, clergy resident in its chapter.

clue.text: Restoration of B. Cowen's predecessor, not fully in ascendancy

indicators.note: in a down entry rising means the letters read upwards
not fully means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: Bertie Ahern was Irish Taoiseach before Brian Cowen

explanation.surface: A return to health for Ireland's former leader, never quite on the rise.
explanation.walkthrough: Bertie Ahern preceded Brian Cowen as Irish prime minister; B. AHERN less N is BAHER, read upwards in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Rehab is short for rehabilitation, restoring someone to health or normal life.

clue.text: Existential being gatecrashing Socrates' seminar

indicators.note: the answer gatecrashes, pushing in across the two words of the phrase

explanation.surface: A philosophical being turns up uninvited at Socrates' class.
explanation.definitionFit: Esse is Latin for to be, used in philosophy for actual existence or essential being.

clue.text: Pulls up teacher's pet

indicators.note: in a down entry up means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: to tow is to pull

explanation.surface: A favourite pupil pulls their socks up.
explanation.definitionFit: A swot is a studious pupil who works hard, often seen as the teacher's favourite.

clue.text: One who went over the edge in 16, sick in the sea at Calais

definitions.text: One who went over the edge in 16

indicators.note: in means one word goes inside the other

parts.note: mer is French for sea, Calais being a French port
ill means sick

explanation.surface: A comedian who fell off a cliff was seasick in the Channel off Calais.
explanation.walkthrough: Jonathan Miller was one of the Beyond the Fringe four; 16 is COMEDY.
explanation.definitionFit: Jonathan Miller performed in the satirical revue Beyond the Fringe, the edge of the fringe.

clue.text: Staying cryptically rendered for this cutter

parts.note: read as tea inside a saying: the T for tea goes into the word for an adage, making the clue word

explanation.surface: A clue writer remarks that staying power is cryptically shown by a cutting tool.
explanation.walkthrough: CHA is tea and SAW is a saying; tea (T) in SAYING gives the clue word 'Staying', so the answer is the wordplay that builds it.
explanation.definitionFit: A chainsaw is a motor-driven saw with teeth on a chain, a tool for cutting wood.

clue.text: Complain persistently to sweet potato farmer, perhaps?

explanation.surface: Grumbling at a farmer of sweet potatoes.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a joke: one who grows yams, a sweet-potato-like tuber, as a farmer farms.
explanation.definitionFit: To yammer is to whine or talk loudly and continuously; the invented sense means a grower of yams.

clue.text: One who went over the edge in 16, clear to see in criminal

definitions.text: One who went over the edge in 16

indicators.note: in means the profit word goes inside the crook word

parts.note: bent is slang for corrupt or criminal
to net is to clear as profit

explanation.surface: A comedian who fell over the edge was plainly crooked.
explanation.walkthrough: Alan Bennett was one of the Beyond the Fringe four; 16 is COMEDY. 'to see' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Bennett wrote and acted in the revue Beyond the Fringe, the edge of the fringe.
